official: An exploration of remote treatment planning for a dental general anaesthetic by specialists in paediatric dentistry a mixed methods study
summary:
Background and study aims
Tooth decay is the most common reason that children are admitted to hospital in the UK. Many children need treatment under a dental general anaesthetic (GA), where they are asleep while dental treatment is carried out. It is important that the correct treatment plan is made before the GA so that all necessary treatment can be completed during a single procedure. If treatment needs are missed, a child may require a second GA, which can be distressing for the child and family and places additional demands on NHS services.

Specialists in paediatric dentistry are trained to assess children who require dental treatment under GA. However, many parts of the UK do not have easy access to these specialists. As a result, treatment planning can vary depending on where a child lives.

This study aims to explore whether specialists in paediatric dentistry can accurately create treatment plans remotely using photographs and dental X-rays, rather than seeing the child in person. The study will also explore how acceptable this approach is to parents, carers and dental specialists, and whether it could help improve access to specialist care in the future.

Who can participate?
Children aged 4 to 16 years who attend Liverpool University Dental Hospital and are planned for dental treatment under general anaesthetic; parents or guardians of participating children; and specialists in paediatric dentistry who work at Liverpool University Dental Hospital.

What does the study involve?
The study has three parts.
In the first part, children attending a routine hospital appointment for treatment planning under general anaesthetic will be invited to take part. Five photographs of their teeth will be taken. No additional X-rays will be required. Routine X-rays already taken as part of their normal care will be used. The child's treatment plan made during the hospital appointment will be recorded.

All identifying information will be removed from the photographs and X-rays before they are uploaded to a secure online platform. Specialists in paediatric dentistry will then review the images remotely and create a treatment plan. Researchers will compare the remote treatment plans with those made during the face-to-face appointment to see how closely they match.

In the second part, parents or guardians of participating children will be invited to take part in an online interview. The interview will explore their views on remote treatment planning and whether they would find this approach acceptable.
In the third part, specialists in paediatric dentistry will take part in discussions and evaluation activities to explore their experiences of using the online platform and identify ways it could be improved.

The study aims to recruit approximately 20 children, 10–15 parents or guardians, and 5 specialists in paediatric dentistry.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants are unlikely to receive a direct benefit from taking part. However, the information gathered may help improve access to specialist paediatric dental services in the future and reduce inequalities in care for children who require treatment under general anaesthesia.

The risks associated with participation are low. Children will only have photographs taken of their teeth, which may take a few minutes during their appointment. No additional dental treatment or X-rays will be required. Parents and specialists who take part in interviews or discussions may be asked to spend additional time sharing their views and experiences. All information collected will be kept confidential and handled in accordance with data protection regulations.

Where is the study run from?
The University of Liverpool and Liverpool University Dental Hospital, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
May 2026 to June 2028. 

Who is funding the study?
The University of Liverpool, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Sarah McKernon, Study Coordinator, University of Liverpool, mckernon@liverpool.ac.uk
conditions: Children/young person aged 4-16 who are treatment planned for a dental general anaesthetic (DGA)

interventions.name: This is a pilot study testing a complex intervention. The first part of the study utilises a custom-built platform. Specialists in paediatric dentistry will use the platform to complete a treatment plan for a child requiring a DGA. The child will have attended a New Patient Consultation appointment

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Children/young person aged 4-16 who are treatment planned for a DGA with radiographs (must have both BW and OPT) taken at the time of consultation 
2. The child/young person lives with a parent/guardian who can consent, this adult needs to be present at the time of child recruitment
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Children who are not able to tolerate intra-oral photographs
2.	Children in care who do not live with someone who can consent for them
3.	Unable to gain translation services for participants spoken language
